title: google-deepmind/alphagenome — This API provides programmatic access to the AlphaGenome model developed by Google DeepMind.
content:
Get API key | Quick start | Installation | Documentation | Community | Terms of Use | Model code
The AlphaGenome API provides access to AlphaGenome, Google DeepMind’s unifying model for deciphering the regulatory code within DNA sequences. This repository contains client-side code, examples and documentation to help you use the AlphaGenome API.
AlphaGenome offers multimodal predictions, encompassing diverse functional outputs such as gene expression, splicing patterns, chromatin features, and contact maps (see diagram below). The model analyzes DNA sequences of up to 1 million base pairs in length and can deliver predictions at single base-pair resolution for most outputs. AlphaGenome achieves state-of-the-art performance across a range of genomic prediction benchmarks, including numerous diverse variant effect prediction tasks (detailed in Avsec et al.).
AlphaGenome API also provides access to the ‘Atlas’ dataset. AlphaGenome Atlas is a resource of pre-computed variant effect score predictions, AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score, and feature importances across the entire human genome. Learn more here.
The API is offered free of charge for non-commercial use (subject to the terms of use). Query rates vary based on demand – the pre-computed Atlas predictions will typically have a larger query rate. Other predictions are better suited for smaller to medium-scale analyses such as analysing a limited number of genomic regions or variants requiring 1000s of predictions, but is likely not suitable for large scale analyses requiring more than 1 million predictions. Once you obtain your API key, you can easily get started by following our Quick Start Guide, or watching our AlphaGenome 101 tutorial.
The documentation also covers a set of comprehensive tutorials, variant scoring
strategies to efficiently score variant effects, and a visualization library to
generate matplotlib figures for the different output modalities.
We cover additional details of the capabilities and limitations in our documentation. For support and feedback:
- Please submit bugs and any code-related issues on GitHub.
- For general feedback, questions about usage, and/or feature requests, please use the community forum – it’s actively monitored by our team so you're likely to find answers and insights faster.
- If you can't find what you're looking for, please get in touch with the AlphaGenome team on alphagenome@google.com and we will be happy to assist you with questions. We’re working hard to answer all inquiries but there may be a short delay in our response due to the high volume we are receiving.
AlphaGenome API is subject to the AlphaGenome Terms of Service. Other than as expressly provided in the AlphaGenome Terms of Service (see references to Permissive Use Downloadable Artifacts for Commercial and Non-Commercial Use), outputs generated by AlphaGenome and other information provided in AlphaGenome Atlas are for non-commercial use only and should not be used for the training of other machine learning models. Predictions are for theoretical modelling and research purposes only. They must not be used for clinical decision-making or relied upon for medical or other professional advice.
AlphaGenome is also available for commercial use via Google Cloud
The quickest way to get started is to run our example notebooks in Google Colab. Here are some starter notebooks:
- Quick start: An introduction to quickly get you started with using the model and making predictions.
- Visualizing predictions: Learn how to visualize different model predictions using the visualization libraries.
Alternatively, you can dive straight in by following the installation guide and start writing code! Here's an example of making a variant prediction:
from alphagenome.data import genome
from alphagenome.models import dna_client
from alphagenome.visualization import plot_components
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
API_KEY = 'MyAPIKey'
model = dna_client.create(API_KEY)
interval = genome.Interval(chromosome='chr22', start=35677410, end=36725986)
variant = genome.Variant(
    chromosome='chr22',
    position=36201698,
    reference_bases='A',
    alternate_bases='C',
)
outputs = model.predict_variant(
    interval=interval,
    variant=variant,
    ontology_terms=['UBERON:0001157'],
    requested_outputs=[dna_client.OutputType.RNA_SEQ],
)
plot_components.plot(
    [
        plot_components.OverlaidTracks(
            tdata={
                'REF': outputs.reference.rna_seq,
                'ALT': outputs.alternate.rna_seq,
            },
            colors={'REF': 'dimgrey', 'ALT': 'red'},
        ),
    ],
    interval=outputs.reference.rna_seq.interval.resize(2**15),
    # Annotate the location of the variant as a vertical line.
    annotations=[plot_components.VariantAnnotation([variant], alpha=0.8)],
)
plt.show()
Tip
You may optionally wish to create a Python Virtual Environment to prevent conflicts with your system's Python environment.
To install alphagenome, clone a local copy of the repository and run pip install:
$ git clone https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphagenome.git
$ pip install ./alphagenome
See the documentation for information on alternative installation strategies.
We welcome bug fixes and some new features to this project. Before sending your pull request, please read the CONTRIBUTING documentation, ensure all tests pass, and that your contributions are formatted correctly.
You can check your changes by running the following from the alphagenome root
directory:
$ python3 -m pip install hatch
$ python3 -m hatch run check:all  # Runs linter and formatter.
$ python3 -m hatch test
If you use AlphaGenome in your research, please cite using:

report.summary: Google DeepMind releases a Python client for AlphaGenome, its DNA regulatory-code model, offering free API access to multimodal genomic predictions at base-pair resolution.
report.background: Only about 2% of the human genome codes for proteins; the rest is regulatory DNA that decides when, where and how strongly genes are switched on. Linking a single DNA letter change to its downstream effect has been a long-standing bottleneck in genetics, especially since most disease-associated variants fall outside protein-coding regions. Earlier models such as Enformer, Basenji and Sei predicted some of these signals, but each covered a narrow set of assays, often at coarse resolution. Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome, published in Nature, unifies many modalities — expression, splicing, chromatin accessibility and 3D contact maps — in one model trained on large functional genomics consortia datasets. This repository wraps that model in a Python client and gRPC API, moving it from paper artifact to something any bioinformatician with an API key can call from a notebook.
key_points: Multimodal, long-range predictions: AlphaGenome accepts DNA sequences up to one million base pairs and returns simultaneous predictions for gene expression, splicing, chromatin features and contact maps, most at single base-pair resolution. That breadth matters because one variant can affect several regulatory layers at once, and analyzing them separately can miss the combined effect. DeepMind claims state-of-the-art results across many diverse variant-effect benchmarks.

Free API, with explicit scale limits: the API is free for non-commercial use once you obtain a key, but DeepMind says it suits analyses in the thousands of predictions, not more than roughly a million. Pre-computed 'Atlas' predictions get a higher query rate. Commercial use runs through Google Cloud, and outputs may not be used to train other machine learning models.

An Atlas of pre-computed genome-wide scores: alongside on-demand predictions, the release exposes the AlphaGenome Atlas — pre-computed variant effect scores, an AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score, and feature importances across the whole human genome. Researchers can therefore look up a variant's predicted impact without running the model themselves, making large candidate-list scans far cheaper.

Developer-friendly client, tutorials and visualization: the repository is client-side code rather than model weights. It ships a pip-installable alphagenome package, Colab notebooks, variant-scoring recipes and a matplotlib visualization library for overlaid reference/alternate tracks. A short snippet creates the client with an API key, defines an Interval and Variant, requests RNA-seq output for a tissue ontology term, and plots the difference. Code is Apache-2.0; docs are CC-BY.

Careful scoping and governance: predictions are labelled for theoretical modelling and research only, explicitly not for clinical decision-making or medical advice, and the project is not an official Google product. Support runs through a monitored community forum and a dedicated email. This framing matters because variant effect predictors are often mistaken for diagnostic tools, and regulators are increasingly attentive to how such models are marketed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AlphaGenome is another sign that domain foundation models — biology, weather, materials — are maturing into API products rather than one-off papers, with Google Cloud as the commercial funnel. For developers, genomics work increasingly resembles ordinary ML engineering: install a package, call a client, get tensors back, no GPU cluster or terabyte training set required, though fluency in genomic formats and vocabularies (intervals, ontology terms, VCF) remains the real barrier. For biologists and clinical researchers, the practical change is speed — testing hundreds of candidate causal variants in an afternoon instead of months of wet-lab assays. The limits are equally clear: no clinical use, no training other models on outputs, and a scale ceiling that pushes the heaviest workloads onto the paid path, so academia gains access while industrial screens still pay.
report.tools: Follow up with the alphagenome Python package and its Colab quick-start and visualization notebooks. Compare results against Enformer, Sei, Borzoi and Ensembl VEP for variant annotation. Pair it with standard tooling: pyfaidx or pysam for sequence handling, pandas and anndata for outputs, Scanpy for expression analysis, and gnomAD or ClinVar to ground predictions in real variant frequencies. For reproducible scoring, read the repository's variant-scoring strategies documentation and explore the pre-computed Atlas release.
